title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure built on synthetic media. An AI generated video was made to show a well known financial figure endorsing an investment with large returns, and that fabricated endorsement was the point of first contact with the victim. The person depicted did not appear in the video, and the endorsement did not exist. The system was not used outside its conditions by accident, it was used to manufacture a testimonial that no real person had given.

The video was only the opening. After a small first payment the contact moved to WhatsApp, the victim was urged to pay more, was given the impression of help, handed remote access to a computer, opened several online accounts, and was encouraged to borrow. Catching it would have required confirming two things the victim had no way to confirm from inside the video: that the figure shown had actually endorsed the investment, and that the financial services provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. The fraud was designed so that neither check happened before the money moved.

What is not established is who was depicted. The Police Service of Northern Ireland did not name the celebrity, so whether the video showed a real identifiable person, and whether that person had any connection to the scheme, is unknown. The report is a police account of a fraud, not a finding against any named party, and no prosecution or verdict is recorded.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 after an artificial intelligence scam, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said. The victim saw an AI generated video that appeared to show a well known financial figure endorsing an investment with large returns. Police did not name the celebrity. BBC News NI said similar scams have used figures such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. After a small first payment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more.

Police called the fraud sophisticated. The criminals persuaded the victim to open several online accounts and gave them remote access to the victim's computer, claiming to help with the investment. The victim was encouraged to borrow money, and the funds went to accounts controlled by the criminals. Superintendent Joanne Gibson urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk to relatives about fraud. Police advised verifying who people are dealing with and checking that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
